Vignette: Rajan

Rajan is a 68-year-old South Asian man who works as a program coordinator for a small non-profit organization that provides housing support to recently arrived refugees. He is soft-spoken and deliberate in his speech, the kind of man who chooses his words carefully and listens more than he talks. He has been divorced for eleven years. He lives alone in a modest apartment, and he describes his life before what happened as quiet but purposeful.

Three years ago, Rajan was sexually assaulted by a man he had known through his professional network - someone he had trusted, someone who had attended the same community fundraisers and shared meals at the same tables. The assault occurred after an evening event, when Rajan accepted a ride home. He does not speak about the details easily. What he does say is that he froze. That he could not understand, in the moment, what was happening to his body. That afterward he sat on the floor of his bathroom for a long time, unable to move, unable to think in any language he recognized as his own.

He never reported it. The reasons for this are layered and he knows it. He is a man of a certain generation, from a culture where what happened to him is not supposed to happen to men - or at least, is not supposed to be spoken of. He worried about his standing in the community. He worried no one would believe him. He worried, in a way that still shames him, that somehow he had failed to prevent it.

In the months that followed, Rajan threw himself into his work with a ferocity that surprised even his colleagues. He organized drives, wrote grant proposals, sat with families who had survived things he could not imagine. He told himself that staying busy was the same as being well. But at night, the work could not follow him home. He stopped sleeping more than two or three hours at a stretch. He would wake with his heart hammering, the smell of that man's cologne somehow present in a room where it had no right to be.

He began to avoid. He stopped attending community events. He declined invitations from colleagues and old friends, offering excuses that were polite and unconvincing. He changed the route he drives to work so he does not pass the street where the assault occurred. When a new volunteer at the non-profit - a large man with a similar build - entered the office unexpectedly one afternoon, Rajan had to excuse himself and stand in the parking lot for twenty minutes, breathing, telling himself where he was and what year it was.

He describes a persistent feeling of being outside himself, of watching his own life from a slight distance, as though he is a guest in it rather than the person living it. He has little interest in the things that used to matter to him - cricket, cooking elaborate meals on Sundays, calling his daughter in Vancouver. He still calls her, but he finds himself unable to say anything real. He does not want her to worry. He does not want her to know.

What brings him to therapy now, after three years, is something small. A refugee family he has been working with - a father and two young sons - recently celebrated their first anniversary in the country. They brought him sweets and embraced him in the office, and Rajan stood there receiving their gratitude and felt absolutely nothing. He drove home and sat in his car for a long time. He had spent his professional life helping people rebuild after devastation, and he could not understand how he had become someone who felt nothing at all. That emptiness frightened him more than the nightmares. It was what finally made him pick up the phone.
